Traveller
trav'el-er
n. (one journeying; the guest Job received, the figure in Nathan's parable, and the men who kept to byways when the highways were unsafe)
From travel, originally the same word as travail — French travail, labour — because a journey was hard work. The Hebrew terms are helek, one who walks, and orach, one on a road.

Biblical Definition

Deborah's song dates the disorder of the period by what happened to travel: “In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways” (Judges 5:6). Empty roads are the mark of a lawless country. Nathan puts a traveller at the centre of the parable that broke David: “And there came a traveller unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him; but took the poor man's lamb” (2 Samuel 12:4). The whole force of the parable rests on a duty everyone in that culture assumed — a guest must be fed — and on the rich man discharging it at his neighbour's expense. Job cites the same duty as evidence of his integrity: “The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller” (Job 31:32). And Jeremiah dares to use the image of God Himself, in a complaint: “why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night?” (Jeremiah 14:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a traveller as one who travels in any way, and notes that travel and travail are the same word, a journey being laborious.

expand to see more

TRAVELLER, n. One who travels in any way.

2. One who visits foreign countries.

TRAVEL, v.i. To journey; to walk or ride to a distant place.

WAYFARING, a. Travelling; passing; being on a journey.

HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 12:4 — "And there came a traveller unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him; but took the poor man's lamb, and dressed it for the man that was come to him."

Job 31:32 — "The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller."

Judges 5:6 — "In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways."

Jeremiah 14:8 — "O the hope of Israel, the saviour thereof in time of trouble, why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night?"

Modern Corruption

Hospitality is reduced to entertaining friends in a tidy house, and Scripture means opening a door to a stranger who cannot repay.

expand to see more

The biblical duty concerns the traveller — a person passing through, unknown, unable to return the favour. Job's boast is that the stranger did not lodge in the street; the elder must be given to hospitality; the Hebrews are told to entertain strangers, since some have entertained angels unawares. Modern hospitality has narrowed almost entirely to hosting people one already knows, in circumstances one controls, which is a good thing and is not the thing commanded. The narrowing has a cost. A congregation that has lost the practice of receiving strangers has also lost the setting in which most of the New Testament's one-another commands were originally obeyed.

Nathan's parable rewards a second look. The rich man was not condemned for refusing hospitality — he provided the meal — but for providing it out of the poor man's flock. Generosity funded by someone else's loss is the precise shape of the sin, which is why David's anger was so hot and Nathan's thou art the man so devastating. The pattern survives wherever an institution or a leader builds a reputation for care on resources extracted from those least able to spare them. The parable was aimed at a king who had taken a man's only wife, and it was framed as a story about a lamb and a guest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew helek, a traveller — 2 Samuel 12:4; orach, a wayfarer — Judges 5:6, Job 31:32; arach, to wander or journey — Jeremiah 14:8.

expand to see more

Hebrew helek — one who walks, a traveller; 2 Samuel 12:4, its notable occurrence in Nathan's parable.

Hebrew orach — a path, and one who travels it; Judges 5:6 and Job 31:32.

Hebrew netibah — a byway, a crooked path; Judges 5:6, where travellers avoided the highways.

Hebrew ger — a stranger, sojourner; Job 31:32, the man Job would not leave in the street.

Hebrews 13:2 states the standing duty: be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.

Usage

"“The travellers walked through byways” — empty highways are the mark of a lawless land."

"“I opened my doors to the traveller” — Job's evidence of integrity."

"The rich man fed the guest, and fed him out of the poor man's flock."
